title: Who should govern artificial intelligence?
summary: The General Assembly debates how the world should govern AI: an expert panel, a global agency, binding rules, sharing skills with developing countries, and protections for voters, creators and children.

committee.name: General Assembly: governing artificial intelligence (practice)
committee.notes: A practice draft written for class; not an adopted UN text. Positions are estimates from the linked UN records.

topic.name: Governing artificial intelligence
topic.notes: Real topic. Practice draft; country positions are estimates taken from the linked sources, and countries without a source are left to the platform's general model.

tags.un_science_panel: Sets up an independent panel of scientists to report on AI
tags.global_agency: Creates a global United Nations agency for AI
tags.binding_rules: Makes the rules for dangerous AI legally binding
tags.ai_capacity: Shares computing power, skills and technology with developing countries
tags.election_safeguards: Labels AI-made content to protect elections
tags.banned_uses: Stops AI uses that break human rights law
tags.copyright_data: Protects copyright and personal data when AI is trained
tags.child_safety: Requires stronger protection for children using AI

preambular.text: Reaffirming the Charter of the United Nations and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights,
Recalling the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and its seventeen Sustainable Development Goals,
Recalling also General Assembly resolution 78/265 on safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence and resolution 78/311 on building artificial intelligence skills in developing countries,
Noting the Global Digital Compact, which the General Assembly adopted in 2024 as part of the Pact for the Future,
Noting that this draft deals only with civilian uses of artificial intelligence and not with weapons,

operative.text: Decides to set up an independent scientific panel of 40 experts from all regions, chosen through an open call by the Secretary-General, to report each year on what artificial intelligence can do and what risks it brings;
Requests the Secretary-General to propose a new United Nations agency for artificial intelligence, able to inspect and approve the most powerful AI systems;
Calls upon all States to agree a treaty that makes rules for the most dangerous AI systems legally binding, instead of relying on voluntary principles;
Urges richer countries to share computing power, training and technology with developing countries, on terms that both sides agree;
Encourages companies to label images, audio and video made by AI, so that voters can tell real material from fake, especially during elections;
Calls upon States to stop using AI systems that cannot be used without breaking human rights law;
Encourages safeguards for copyright and for personal data when AI systems are trained on books, art and online posts;
Urges States to require stronger protection for children who use AI tools, including age checks and the removal of harmful content.

cards.text: Invites States to share, on a voluntary basis, how they test the most powerful AI systems for safety, and requests the scientific panel to summarise these reports each year;
Requests the Secretary-General to explore whether existing United Nations bodies could cover advanced AI before any new agency is proposed;
Decides that the most powerful AI systems may not be released until they have passed an independent safety test agreed by States;
Requests the scientific panel to include in each report advice on how developing countries can use AI safely, and calls upon donors to fund a shared training programme;
Encourages States to build on their existing national safety guidelines and to share what works, leaving each State free to choose how to apply them;
Calls upon companies to be open about the kinds of books, art and posts used to train AI systems, and to let creators opt out;
Urges States to teach students and parents how to spot AI-made content and how to report harmful material, alongside labels used during elections;
Calls upon States to publish a list of AI uses they have stopped because they conflict with human rights law, and to review that list every two years;

events.title: A regional group meets over the draft
events.body: A regional group meets to compare its views on the draft. Delegates who have spent time with them come away feeling listened to.
events.teaches: Regional groups coordinate their positions before votes, and delegates who listen to them often earn their trust.

events.title: A delegation describes its skills gap
events.body: A delegation from a small island state tells the room how hard it is to train engineers for AI. Delegates who back sharing skills are keener to talk.
events.teaches: Personal accounts in the chamber can move a debate more than general principles do.

events.title: An expert explains voluntary versus binding rules
events.body: An invited expert explains to delegates how voluntary guidelines differ from legally binding treaties, and how long each takes to agree.
events.teaches: Treaties bind only the States that join them and take years to agree; voluntary guidelines are faster but depend on goodwill.

events.title: A capital sends new instructions overnight
events.body: A capital sends fresh instructions to its delegation overnight, and several delegates must rework their plans before they can meet you.
events.teaches: Delegates represent their governments, so instructions from a capital can change a position at short notice.

events.title: A co-sponsor offers a joint meeting
events.body: A co-sponsor of an earlier AI resolution invites delegates to a joint meeting just outside the chamber. Talking to others is easier this turn.
events.teaches: Informal meetings outside the chamber are where much of the real bargaining at the UN takes place.

events.title: An NGO hosts a side event on children and AI
events.body: A children's rights organisation hosts a side event in the lobby. Delegates who attend thank you for raising the issue, and your standing grows.
events.teaches: NGOs cannot vote, but they brief delegates and can shape what ends up on the table.
